title: Al-Muhaymin, the Guardian over all
hook: the Guardian over all, who watches and protects, and a bedtime verse taught by a thief
tomorrow: watched over, yes. but what about the moment you feel weak?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Mu'min: the Giver of Security, and a heart between fear and hope. Secure in him. Today, a name with its ear to the door.
screen: `SECURE IN HIM.` → `AN EAR TO THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: A floorboard creaks at midnight. A parent's footsteps stop outside a child's door, listen to the breathing, and move on. The child never hears it. Yesterday's question was who's awake while you sleep. The Qur'an answers in the verse a hadith in Bukhari ties to bedtime: Ayat al-Kursi, the Verse of the Throne. In Pickthall's words it opens: Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive, the Eternal. Neither slumber nor sleep overtaketh Him.
screen: `FOOTSTEPS AT MIDNIGHT.` → `WHO'S AWAKE?` → `NEITHER SLUMBER NOR SLEEP.`

segments.voice: That's today's name in action. Al-Muhaymin, in Pickthall's list from Surah al-Hashr, is the Guardian: the one who watches over, witnesses, and protects. Say it slowly and listen: mu-hay-min. Bukhari tells how the verse became a bedtime one. Abu Hurayrah was guarding the charity food when a thief came at night, three nights running. On the last night the thief bargained: let me go and I'll teach you words. When you go to bed, recite Ayat al-Kursi, and a guardian from Allah will stay with you, and no devil will come near you till morning. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, told Abu Hurayrah: he told you the truth, though he's a liar. That's the line to tell a friend tonight: a bedtime verse was passed on by a thief, and the Prophet said it was true. The word turns up for the Book as well. Surah al-Ma'idah calls the Qur'an a watcher over the scripture before it, using the same word. Watched over, here, doesn't mean spied on. It means kept, all night, by someone who doesn't sleep.
screen: `AL-MUHAYMIN: THE GUARDIAN.` · `A THIEF, THREE NIGHTS RUNNING.` · `HE TOLD YOU THE TRUTH.` · `KEPT, NOT SPIED ON.` · then, large: `WATCHED OVER.`

segments.voice: Stay still and listen for the quietest sound in the room: a fridge, a fan, someone breathing nearby. Keep your attention on it the way someone keeps watch at a door. For the sit, let that small, steady sound be the one thing you guard.
Al-Muhaymin: the Guardian over all, who watches, witnesses and protects, awake while everyone sleeps.
The line tonight: watched over, all night long, by someone who never needs to sleep. Rest well.

howItsDone: Following the hadith in Bukhari, many Muslims recite Ayat al-Kursi before sleep, and parents often recite it over their children at bedtime.

myth: in Bukhari's story, an angel taught the bedtime verse
a thief taught it, and the Prophet said: he told you the truth, though he's a liar.
Ayat al-Kursi says Allah is never overtaken by sleep
neither slumber nor sleep overtaketh Him.
being watched over by the Guardian means being spied on
the name means watching, witnessing and protecting: kept, all night.

fork.setup: your little brother has been scared of the dark since a creepy video. he asks if anyone's awake while he sleeps. what could you tell him from today?
options: a verse says sleep never overtakes Allah; the Guardian is awake all night.
only people who never do anything wrong get watched over at night.
being scared is babyish; he just needs to stop watching those videos.
fork.reveal: neither slumber nor sleep overtaketh Him, and the bedtime hadith promises a guardian till morning. a sentence a kid can hold.

original.note: Arabic: the Guardian, who watches over, witnesses and protects.

trapdoor: what you thought: a God who watches to catch you out.
what it means: the Guardian who stays awake and keeps you, all night.
what a scholar hears: muhaymin also names the Qur'an as a watcher over earlier scripture; Bukhari's thief story ties the guarding to Ayat al-Kursi.
guess: the Guardian who watches over and protects
the Judge who writes down every wrong done
the Light that shines on the Day of Judgment

chat.says: couldn't sleep. dadi was at my door reciting, like when i was little. do i tell her i heard?
options: Tell her. Ask her to teach you what she recites, so it goes to Chicago too.
Don't. It's private, and saying something would just make it awkward.
Tell her you're grown now, so she doesn't need to watch over you anymore.
chat.meaning: Ayat al-Kursi at bedtime is a way of being watched over by Al-Muhaymin. Learning it from her carries that guarding with you.
